newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's 1997 legislature to meet in China.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's 1997 legislature to meet in China.

text.p: Hong Kong's leader-designate Tung Chee-hwa said on Monday the Beijing-appointed legislature set up to replace the elected Legislative Council in mid-1997 would hold its first sitting soon, in China rather than Hong Kong.
Tung was speaking after his first informal meeting with the post-colonial deputies who will take over lawmaking in Hong Kong when Britain hands back the territory at midnight next June 30.

With only 183 days left until the handover, Tung is moving quickly to assemble a cabinet and to hammer out his relationship with the provisional chamber, which he said would hold its first official session in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

"The provisional legislature must meet for the first time. It'll probably be in Shenzhen. It would be very soon," Tung told reporters after dining the provisional legislature. "We also discussed very unofficially the tasks ahead for the provisional legislature."

Having secured the crucial agreement over the weekend from Hong Kong's influential and popular chief civil servant Anson Chan that she would serve beyond the transition, the 59-year-old Chief Executive-designate's next task is to meet the powerful heads of department of Hong Kong's civil service, the driving force behind the running of the territory of six million people.
China's grip is waxing and British influence waning dramatically as the clock counts down to the end of over 150 years of colonial rule.

The 60-member Provisional Legislature was selected this month by a 400-strong caucus of Hong Kong people vetted by China in order to replace the current elected chamber and undo recent democratic reforms sponsored by the British.
The same body also selected Tung as post-1997 leader.
The provisional legislature is adamantly opposed by Hong Kong's Democratic Party, which emerged as the strongest party in 1995 elections but will be kicked out of office on July 1.
They say the provisional body is a travesty of democracy and will be illegal if it functions before the change of flag. Their threats of legal action have forced the body to meet in China.
The Democrats boycotted the selection process for the chief executive and a provisional legislature, calling it undemocratic because Hong Kong's electorate had no say in it and no vote.
But they have offered Tung qualified cooperation in the form of a "honeymoon on probation".
Tung said on Monday he had agreed to a meeting with the Democratic Party although no date had been set.
Tung also urged Hong Kong's 180,000 civil servants to face the reality of the provisional legislature although he promised to respect their political neutrality in the countdown period.
"The political neutrality of the civil service is very important, we must respect that. But after 1997, the provisional legislature will work with the civil service. That's a reality."
Tung's decision to invite Chan, Hong Kong's Chief Secretary, to stay in her post after the handover, and her acceptance is widely regarded as a positive sign in Hong Kong.
He is expected to meet top civil servants individually in the next few days to select the key members of his future administration and report his decision to Beijing.

In one of the first signs of a crack in the top echelons, chief graft buster Michael Leung, head of the Independent Commission Against Corruption, last week announced he would not serve beyond the handover.

Tung, who met Leung on Monday, said he had not managed to persuade Leung to change his mind. "It is a real pity. I wish he would stay ... but he explained that it was for personal reasons he was leaving," he said.
